content: Cystitis is defined as inflammation of the urinary bladder. When caused by an infection, it is classified as a type of lower urinary tract infection (UTI). The condition most commonly arises from ascending infections originating in the urethra, but it can also result from descending infections via the bloodstream or lymphatic system. While cystitis is more prevalent in women, it can affect individuals of any gender and age group. The urinary tract has been recognized as a site of infection since ancient times, with descriptions dating back to 1550 BC in the Ebers Papyrus. The first documented cases of interstitial cystitis without bladder stones were published in 1836, and the term interstitial cystitis was introduced by Dr. Alexander Skene in 1887. Cystitis can be classified based on its etiology and therapeutic approach into subtypes such as traumatic, interstitial, eosinophilic, hemorrhagic, and cystitis cystica. For treatment purposes, it is further categorized into acute uncomplicated, complicated, and recurrent cystitis. It can also be classified as bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic depending on the causative pathogen. Cystitis occurs when the normally sterile lower urinary tract (urethra and bladder) becomes infected by bacteria, leading to irritation and inflammation. Women are more susceptible due to their shorter urethra, which allows bacteria to reach the bladder more easily. Complicated cystitis often results from urinary obstruction and stasis, which facilitate bacterial growth. Escherichia coli (E. coli), a bacterium found in the lower gastrointestinal tract, is responsible for over 85% of cystitis cases. Other causes include certain medications, diabetes, Crohn's disease, iatrogenic factors, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, urinary obstruction, and bladder incontinence. Cystitis must be distinguished from other causes of dysuria, such as pyelonephritis, urethritis, prostatitis, vulvovaginitis, urethral strictures, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and neoplasms of the bladder, prostate, or kidneys. Approximately 50% of patients with acute uncomplicated cystitis recover without treatment within a few days to weeks. However, untreated cystitis can lead to recurrent infections, pyelonephritis, hematuria, and, in rare cases, renal failure. The prognosis is generally favorable, with most patients experiencing no recurrence or complications after treatment. Patients with cystitis typically appear well, and common physical findings include fever and suprapubic tenderness. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for cystitis, with treatment tailored to the disease course (acute uncomplicated vs. complicated) and local resistance patterns. Preventative measures include abstinence from sexual activity, use of barrier contraception, increased fluid intake, frequent urination, and estrogen therapy for postmenopausal women. Urinary tract infections are more common in women than men, with over 30% of women experiencing at least one episode of cystitis. Of these, 20% will have recurrent infections. The female-to-male ratio for cystitis is approximately 4:1, and acute uncomplicated cystitis is most common in women aged 18–39 years. There is no racial predilection for cystitis, and it is a globally prevalent condition. Risk factors for cystitis include female gender, sexual intercourse, diabetes, pregnancy, catheterization, fecal incontinence, advanced age, and immobility. Certain foods, such as vitamin C, coffee, tea, carbonated and alcoholic beverages, citrus fruits, and spicy foods, may also increase the risk. Routine screening for cystitis is not recommended in the general population. However, screening for bacteriuria is indicated during pregnancy, prior to urologic surgery, or for research purposes. The natural history of cystitis shows that approximately half of patients with acute uncomplicated cystitis recover spontaneously. If untreated, some may develop complications such as recurrent infections, pyelonephritis, hematuria, or renal failure. The prognosis is generally good, with most patients responding well to treatment. The diagnosis of acute uncomplicated cystitis is primarily clinical, based on symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain. Atypical presentations may require urinalysis and urine culture for confirmation. Laboratory findings consistent with cystitis include pyuria, white blood cells (WBCs), red blood cells (RBCs), and a positive urine culture. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, ultrasound, CT scans, and MRI, are not routinely used for diagnosing cystitis. However, they may be employed in specific cases, such as emphysematous cystitis or to detect tumors, stones, or structural abnormalities. Cystoscopy is not typically performed but may be indicated in recurrent or complicated cases. Treatment of cystitis often involves antimicrobial therapy, with the choice of antibiotics guided by the disease course and local resistance patterns. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be used for hemorrhagic cystitis associated with radiation exposure or emphysematous cystitis. Surgical intervention is rarely required and is reserved for underlying pathologies such as tumors or stones causing bladder obstruction. Primary prevention strategies include voiding after intercourse, using barrier contraception, increasing fluid intake, and estrogen therapy in postmenopausal women. Prophylactic antibiotics may be considered for patients with recurrent cystitis associated with sexual activity. Secondary prevention focuses on addressing structural defects or underlying conditions like diabetes to prevent recurrent infections.
